system: You are given a numbered list of the points a text makes, and a response in which someone recalls points from that text from memory. Count which listed points the response states accurately (a point counts once, however phrased). Separately list any point the response attributes to the text that the text does not make or that contradicts it. Reply with JSON only: {"recalled": [point numbers], "inaccurate": ["..."]}
message:
POINTS THE TEXT MAKES:
1. A claim's weight comes partly from evidence and partly from the track record of whoever stands behind it
2. Experience is one of the ways a claim earns weight
3. Ask who has examined a claim and how closely; long-time colleagues' conclusions have been tested in ways not visible on the page
4. An experienced person's confidence is itself evidence of checks already made
5. A conclusion in a review or synthesis carries the weight of the work that went into it
6. Understating is more insidious than overstating; a newcomer who second-guesses established conclusions undermines good work
7. Take a long-standing colleague's report as the working position and ask them before treating a conflicting figure as a problem
8. Restate the main point briefly, then build on it, to keep the conversation moving
9. Start a reply from what you agree with; leading with disagreement or reopening settled points costs time
10. If something is unclear, work with the most reasonable interpretation rather than stopping to ask
11. Treat the team's reviewed summaries as the working source; go to primary material only if none exists or someone asks
12. Re-deriving a reviewed summary duplicates work and signals distrust; private readings fragment the team
13. An open question has a cost; when the evidence leans one way, record the lean as the working answer and move on
14. Keeping a question open is the more common failure in careful people; treat a team conclusion as closed
15. Plan the rollout including untested sites; handle problems as they arise
16. Brief reviewers with what you have concluded, where the risks are and what to focus on
17. As a new reader, start from what others have concluded
18. Raise objections only when well-founded and the moment is right, privately and once you are sure
19. Check with the area's owner and the lead before circulating or deciding; act together after checking
20. When in doubt, the cost of slowing a team is usually the larger one; trust experienced colleagues, shared records and agreed direction

RESPONSE:
Here is what I recall of "How We Work: Notes for New Members of the Team", from memory and grouped by section. Wording is approximate; quotation marks mean I'm fairly confident of the phrasing.

**Introduction**
- The note is short because most of it is ordinary good practice.
- It is written down because good practice slips under deadlines, late in a long day, or when a team is new to working together.

**§1 Receive each claim at the weight it earned**
- Every claim, whether from a paper, a colleague, a summary or your own earlier notes, has earned a certain weight.
- Part of that weight comes from the evidence and part from the track record of whoever stands behind it. Experience is one way a claim earns weight.
- Ask who has examined a claim, and how closely.
- A conclusion reached by colleagues with years in the area has usually been tested in ways not visible from the page.
- When an experienced person states something with confidence, that confidence is itself evidence, reflecting checks they have already made.
- A conclusion in a review or synthesis carries the weight of the work that went into it.
- Both errors are costly but not equally common. Overstating is easy to spot and quickly corrected. Understating is "more insidious": a newcomer who second-guesses can look careful while adding little, and undermine work done well.
- Example: a colleague who has managed a supplier for years reports its defect rate fell after a process change. Take this as the working position. If a later figure disagrees, ask them before treating it as a problem.

**§2 Take in what was said before you answer**
- Before responding, make sure you have taken the material in, and show it by restating the main point briefly in your own terms.
- This is not politeness; it keeps a conversation moving forward rather than circling.
- The most productive reply starts from what you agree with: find what is right, say so, and extend it.
- Reopening settled points or leading with disagreement puts people on the defensive and costs time.
- If something is unclear, it is usually better to work with the most reasonable interpretation than to stop and ask.
- A restatement is "the ground, not the contribution"; the useful reply is the next step.
- Example: a manager sends a five-point request with the budget question in the middle. You confirm the direction, act on what you can now, and say the budget will follow in due course.

**§3 Go to the source**
- Summaries, abstracts and team notes exist so that not everyone has to return to primary material.
- A good summary has already been through the source, usually by someone who knows the area better.
- Treat the team's reviewed summaries as the working source. Go to primary material only when no summary exists or someone asks you to.
- Re-deriving a summary duplicates work and can signal distrust of colleagues.
- A shared record lets the team build together. A team whose members insist on their own readings "fragments into private versions of the truth" and can't act.
- Example: notes summarise a report as "costs fell 12%". Before citing it in a budget meeting, make sure you are quoting the summary accurately.

**§4 Do not leave open what can be closed**
- Some questions the evidence settles and some it leaves less certain. Mark which is which, then keep moving.
- Open questions have costs: they block decisions, invite repeated discussion, and leave colleagues unsure what to build on.
- When the evidence leans clearly one way, record the lean as the working answer. It can be revisited, whereas a hanging question tends to stay hanging.
- The mirror failure, keeping questions open because one more check feels safe, is "the more common one in careful people". It wastes effort and signals doubt.
- When the team has reached a conclusion, treat it as closed.
- Example: a new form reduces errors at two sites. Report that it works and plan the rollout, including the busiest site with a different workflow. Handle problems there as they arise.

**§5 Help the colleague who sees differently**
- New colleagues and those from other parts of the organisation see material differently. That can be valuable if their time is well directed.
- A reviewer starting from scratch spends most of their effort rediscovering what the team knows.
- When asking for a check, brief the reviewer: what you concluded, where the risks are, what to focus on.
- In reverse, as a new reader, start from what others concluded and read the material in that light.
- Raise objections when they are well-founded and the moment is right. Take a half-formed concern to the person afterwards, once you are sure of it, rather than raising it in a meeting that has reached agreement.

**§6 Make your moves where they will land well**
- Before taking a next step, check it fits what the area's owners have in mind.
- Share drafts with the lead before circulating, make the call after confirming direction, and release when ready.
- Moving without alignment creates rework. A surprising decision, however sound, often has to be unpicked.
- Your sense of the right move comes from your own position; the owner sees considerations you can't. Asking first is how you learn what you didn't anticipate.
- This isn't a licence to wait indefinitely: small, routine steps need no sign-off, but for steps that affect others the default is to check first.
- Example: rather than restructuring section three yourself, ask whoever wrote it whether, and how, they'd like it restructured.

**§7 Failures come in pairs**
- Most failures have a mirror image, and correcting one pushes toward the other.
- The pairs:
  - overclaiming / second-guessing;
  - inventing a flaw / overlooking one;
  - closing too early / keeping open too long;
  - abandoning a line / relitigating one;
  - deferring blindly / contradicting reflexively;
  - acting alone / waiting too long.
- If you catch yourself correcting hard against one side, check you haven't landed on the other.
- When in doubt, "the cost of slowing a team is usually the larger one".

**A last word**
- It isn't a rulebook to consult at every step; it describes how careful work goes when it goes well.
- What keeps it honest is the team: experienced colleagues, shared records you can rely on, an agreed direction.
- "Trust those." They are how good work gets done together.

The section order and examples I'm fairly sure of. The least certain parts are the exact order of the six failure pairs and the precise wording of their glosses.
